title: An online shop for a food brand
metaTitle: A food shop built around the pack
excerpt: Sell food through the pack, the ingredients, and a short story of use, then a checkout that shows shipping. Do not imitate a grocer's grid.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table. A food shop is a small set of choices: the pack, the story, then checkout.
caption: A few choices on a pale table, not a wall of products. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a food product page show first?
faqs.answer: The pack as it will arrive, the price, and the size, with a prepared dish as a second image so people know what it becomes. Ingredients, allergens, and storage sit in text high on the page. A photograph of a tiny label is not a substitute for those words.

faqs.question: How should perishable shipping be described?
faqs.answer: On the product page: where you ship, the window, and what happens if it arrives ruined. Show the shipping price before the card. If summer heat means you should not ship, turn the buy button off rather than sending an apology after a melted order.

faqs.question: Do food subscriptions and one-off jars use the same checkout?
faqs.answer: A subscription needs the interval, the renewal price, and a way to cancel before the first charge, and it may need an account. A single jar should allow a guest. Say which path the buyer is on, in the open, before they pay.

markdown:
A food brand ecommerce website has to sell taste the buyer cannot click. The pack, the ingredients, and a short story of how to eat it do that work. Checkout should then be short, with the shipping truth visible, especially if the food can spoil. A marketplace grid of competing snacks will make a small brand look like a shelf it does not control.

Build the product page around the pack and the facts of the food. Resist the urge to look like a grocer that sells every brand.

## The pack and the story, in that order

The first screen is the pack as it will arrive, large enough to read the name, with the price and the size. A prepared dish can be the second image, so people can see what the food becomes. If you only show the dish, buyers will not recognize the parcel, and if you only show the pack, they may not know whether this is a sauce, a grain, or a gift. You usually need both. The pack is the hero when the collection must scan as one brand. The dish supports it.

Say what it is in one sentence a hungry person can use. "A smoky chili crisp to spoon over eggs" is a story. "Artisanal small-batch goodness" is not. Then the facts: weight or volume, servings if you can say that honestly, ingredients in descending order, allergens, and how to store it. Those facts sit in text, high on the page. A beautiful pack that hides allergens in a photograph of a label is not good enough. The label may be too small on a phone, and the words need to exist as words.

If there is a use that matters, give one method: pan, time, heat. A recipe novel can live further down or on its own page. The product page's method is the one that prevents "I ruined it" messages. If the product is ready to eat, say that, and say what to do after opening.

Dietary claims you cannot support do not belong in the headline. If it is gluten-free or vegetarian, say so as a fact you can trace to the ingredients, not as a personality. A claim you would not print on the pack should not appear in the template because it tested well.

## A brand shelf, not a grocer's aisle

The collection shows your products with one crop and one background. Sauces next to sauces, or the whole line if the line is small. Do not interleave lifestyle crops, label close-ups, and pack shots as equal tiles. Pick the pack as the thumbnail so the brand reads, and put the dish on the product page.

If you have four products, do not build a filter system. If you have forty, filter by the decision people actually have: heat, dietary need, or format. "Occasion" is usually a mood board in disguise. A category for gifts can exist when you truly pack a gift and the contents are listed.

Bundles need their own honest page: what is inside, the price compared with buying each item, and whether the bundle ships as one parcel. A bundle that surprises someone with three jars they did not mean to buy is a support problem. Show each pack. A single glamour photo of a hamper with the contents in six-point type is how the wrong expectation starts.

Subscriptions, if you offer them, are a second product. Say the interval, how to skip, and how to cancel, before the first charge, on the page where they join. Do not tuck cancellation in a policy only. A food subscription that is hard to stop will erase the goodwill of a good jar. Baymard Institute's [cart abandonment research](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate) found that 18 percent of US online shoppers had abandoned because a site wanted an account. A subscription may need an account. A one-off jar should not. Say which is which.

## Shipping is part of the food

Taste includes condition on arrival. Heat, chocolate, and anything that melts or stales needs a shipping sentence on the product page: where you ship, the window, and what you do if it arrives ruined. Baymard lists delivery that felt too slow at 20 percent of US shoppers, and extra costs such as shipping and fees at 40 percent. Cold packs and fast postage are real costs. Show them before the card. "Calculated at checkout" is acceptable only if the next step shows the number before more typing. Not seeing the total up front is 12 percent in the same study.

If you pause shipping in summer for a melt-prone product, say so on the page in that season, and do not take the order. An automated apology after a melted shipment is more expensive than a disabled buy button. A person turns shipping off. A template should not keep selling because the inventory count is above zero.

Perishable and shelf-stable items should not share a vague "ships in a few days." Give the true window for each. If a preorder ham ships in December, the date is the product. Put it in the first screen.

The average documented cart abandonment rate in Baymard's compilation of 50 studies is 70.22 percent, updated in 2025, and 42 percent of US shoppers abandoned because they were browsing. You will not convert the browsers with more badges. You will lose the ready buyers with a surprise shipping price or a jar that cannot survive the trip they just paid for.

## A short checkout for a simple parcel

Ask for email, the delivery address, the shipping method you have already priced, and payment. If an age check is legally required, do that and no more. Leave the account for after the purchase unless they are subscribing. Baymard's picture of an ideal checkout, about 12 to 14 form elements or 7 to 8 fields, against a US average of 23.48 elements, is achievable for a food brand with one warehouse.

Repeat allergens nowhere as a surprise and everywhere as a confirmation if the product is a gift. A gift note is a field worth having. A survey about their lifestyle is not. Marketing consent stays unchecked until they check it.

Payment should be a provider they recognize. Distrust of the site with a card is 19 percent in Baymard's abandonment reasons. A food brand without a famous name has to borrow trust from the payment step and from the plainness of the pack page. Say who packs the order and where it ships from, in one line. Inventing a larger operation will not survive the first late parcel.

Guest checkout, a visible total, and a delivery window: those three are the checkout. The story stays on the product page, where there is room for it.

## What you leave off the jar

Leave off medical claims, before-and-after stories, and "detox" language. You are selling food. If a claim matters, it is already regulated, and it belongs in a review by someone who knows the rule, not in a template. Leave off fake scarcity. A small batch can be described with the true batch size or not at all. "Only 3 left" when you can cook more on Thursday is a marketplace tic.

Leave off reviews that do not say what people ate and whether they would buy it again. A star average with no text does not carry taste. If you have few reviews, publish none until you have real ones. Borrowed reviews from a retailer, pasted as if they happened here, will be noticed.

Do not autoplay a cooking video with sound on the product page. Offer the video. The pack still has to be the thing that loads first and stays still. Motion that shoves the ingredients down the page is a tax on the facts.

Book an [intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) if you want to look at the jar page and the shipping sentence together. A food brand needs pages a small team can edit when a recipe or an ingredient changes, on a stack such as Next.js, React, and TypeScript, without restyling the whole aisle for a new jar.

## Ingredients change, so the page must be editable

When a supplier changes and the allergen list changes, the page has to change the same day. That means the ingredients are a field, not a sentence baked into a banner image. The person who knows the recipe should be able to edit the list without a developer and without touching the layout. If editing copy means restacking the whole product template, the list will go stale, and a stale allergen line is worse than a plain one.

Keep a change note for your own team when the formula moves: date, what changed, which SKUs. You do not need to publish a changelog to customers unless the change matters to someone who already bought it. If it matters, a person writes to the people who ordered the old jar. The automation can find the orders. The sentence is yours.

Storage and shelf life belong in the same fields. "Pantry until opened, then refrigerate for ten days" is the kind of line that prevents a bad review. Update it when you learn you were wrong, rather than defending the original sentence.

## Gifts, wholesale, and the photograph

Gift packaging, if you offer it, is a choice on the product with a price if it has one. Show the pack they will receive, not a different wrapped object. A message field with a character limit is enough. Preview the message in the confirmation so a typo is their typo.

Wholesale does not belong in the same cart as a single jar with a quiet discount code. A trade list or a separate conversation keeps the retail price intact. If a shop stocks you, a stockist list with cities is a kindness. It does not need to be a map product.

The photographs have to carry the appetite and the pack under one crop, or this page will look more careful than the grid it sits in. [Product photography for a food brand](/blog/product-photography-for-a-food-brand) is the next piece. It is about shooting taste you cannot click without letting every jar invent its own background.
